name: Frequency illusion
statement: Once someone notices a word or an object for the first time, they see it everywhere, and read their own new attention as a rise in how often it occurs.
meaning: The claim has two halves and only one of them is usually checked. The first half is about attention: a thing newly learned becomes salient, so more of its occurrences get registered. The second half is a judgement, that the thing is now happening more often than it was. Zwicky's 2005 post calls the illusion a selective attention effect. His 2006 abstract adds confirmation bias, looking for cases that fit and passing over the rest. This atlas covers those two mechanisms on their own pages, under selective perception, entry 174, and confirmation bias, entry 5, and covers the sister coinage from the same post under recency illusion, entry 259. Testing the frequency claim needs two numbers in one study: what a person believes the rate is, and what the rate actually is. Nearly all of the writing about this bias supplies the first and asserts the second.

origin.note: Zwicky named the Frequency Illusion in "Just between Dr. Language and I", which closes by calling itself a lightly edited version of a posting to the American Dialect Society mailing list of the same day. The older name is 11 years older and comes from a reader item in the Bulletin Board column of the St Paul Pioneer Press, 16 October 1994, signed with the pen name 'Gigetto on Lincoln'. Neither text is peer reviewed, and neither reports a measurement.

evidence: Three documents carry the origin of the idea and none of them counts anything. The 1994 Bulletin Board item states a rule: the first time you learn a new word, phrase or idea, you will see it again in print within 24 hours, topical things excepted. It supports the rule with one anecdote about the Baader-Meinhof gang. Zwicky's 2005 post offers a demonstration rather than an experiment. A Stanford group studying the quotative 'all', as in the song title "I'm like 'yeah' and she's all 'no'", believed the form was common in the speech of young Californians, and the undergraduates on the project reported friends who used it "all the time". Those friends were recorded, the conversations transcribed and the quotatives extracted. Quotative 'all' turned out to be very low in frequency while quotative 'like' was common. The post gives no rates, no sample size and no test. The counts reached print two years later, in a paper Zwicky co-wrote with John Rickford, Thomas Wasow and Isabelle Buchstaller. Their 2005 Stanford Tape-Recorded Corpus yielded 544 quotatives, of which 23, or 4.2%, were 'all', against 375 tokens of 'like'. His 2006 abstract restates the definition and credits selective attention and confirmation bias, again with no data. The one quantitative survey located tests a different population. Van der Meulen searched a database of 5,678 entries from Dutch prescriptive publications dated 1900 to 2018. It holds 238 entries carrying recency statements about 341 usage items, and 1,249 entries carrying 1,786 frequency statements. He checked 18 lexical frequency claims against usage corpora and rated all but one an illusion, the exception being meer of mindere mate, whose condemned variant took 76.7% of its variable. Seven grammatical items drew 24 statements, of which 21 fell below his threshold. That threshold is 73%, the mean reading Dutch respondents gave the word vaak, or 'often', in a survey by Willems, Albers and Smeets.

replication.headline: No replication attempt was found, and there is no original experiment to repeat: the effect was named in a blog post that reports no measurements.
replication.detail: The nearest thing to a measurement of Zwicky's own case is the American Speech paper he co-wrote in 2007. It puts quotative 'all' at 4.2% of 544 quotatives in the 2005 Stanford corpus, against colleagues who had reported hearing it all the time. That is a count of one form in one corpus, not a test of what anyone believed the rate to be, and the paper names the recency illusion rather than the frequency illusion. Van der Meulen's Dutch survey checks published frequency claims against corpora, which makes it a first test rather than a repeat. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OSF preprints and Semantic Scholar found no study measuring a person's estimate of a rate against the rate itself, before and after a first exposure.

limits: The searches behind this verdict were re-run on 17 August 2026. Crossref by title and by bibliographic query, under both names, returned optics, ophthalmology and German history. PubMed returned nothing for either phrase in titles and abstracts. Europe PMC returned 11 records for 'frequency illusion' and 19 for 'Baader-Meinhof', among them a dermatology review, a radiology letter, a Cureus case report on a Dieulafoy's lesion and a narrative review of psychological contagion. A title search of OSF preprints returned nothing under either name, and the four papers citing van der Meulen at Semantic Scholar are linguistic. One OpenAlex query was refused for want of an account balance and was not retried. Provenance has its own gaps. Van der Meulen was read in full from the PDF in Radboud University's repository, because MDPI's own site refused every request made here, and its figures were confirmed against a second download. The 1994 item was read on the Pioneer Press website, which dates it 16 October 1994 and marks it updated on 17 April 2021; the print page was not inspected, and the OED places it at page 12, column 2 of the Express section. The pen name is attributed to Terry Mullen by Ben Zimmer in 2019, on the word of Dan Kelly, the feature editor who published the submission. The supporting document is an email signed Terry Mullen, quoted by Alan Bellows in a comment on his own Damn Interesting post on 18 October 2006. No 1994 document carrying Mullen's own name was located. Zwicky's abstract is dated September 2006 and names no venue; its filename and his own index of illusion postings are the only sign that it was written for a Linguistic Society of America meeting. Fiedler and Armbruster's 1994 paper and Begg and colleagues' 1986 paper were verified at Crossref and not read, the American Psychological Association's site having refused this machine.
misreadings: The origin story is usually told wrong in the same way. Retellings place the 1994 coinage on an online message board, when the Bulletin Board was a reader column in a printed newspaper, which is what its name meant in 1994. Wikipedia carried the message board version, uncited, until Terence Eden traced the item and corrected the article in June 2023. The corrected text was still in place when this entry was checked. Bellows's own article still dates the coinage to a Pioneer Press discussion thread circa 1995 and Zwicky's term to 2006. The 1994 claim is also narrower and stronger than the one it is quoted for: seeing an obscure new word again in print within 24 hours, not a general sense that something is now everywhere. Zwicky's account of the mechanism, selective attention plus confirmation bias, is often passed on as a research finding. It is his own explanation, given in a blog post and a conference abstract with no data behind it. The founding example is also read as a pure illusion, and the numbers make it partly a matter of timing. Quotative 'all' led the system among the Californian adolescents Ann Wimmer recorded in 1990 and Carmen Fought in 1994, at 113 of 246 quotations, or 45.9%. By 2005 it was 4.2%, and the paper concludes that the form is in decline after peaking in the 1990s. A belief about frequency can be out of date rather than wrong from the start. Experiments on frequency estimation get folded in as though they had tested this effect. Fiedler and Armbruster's paper carries the words 'frequency illusions' in its title but was published in April 1994, 11 years before Zwicky's coinage, and its title names category-split effects. Wikipedia's article cites a laboratory study of inflation perception by Georganas, Healy and Li, run on 186 undergraduates at Ohio State; that paper mentions neither Zwicky nor the frequency illusion. The OED's entry, added in March 2019, records that people use the phrase and what they mean by it. It is a fact about the language, not a measurement of the effect.

sources.text: Zwicky, A. (2005). Just between Dr. Language and I. Language Log, 7 August 2005. The post that coined 'Frequency Illusion'; a blog post, not a peer-reviewed venue. Read in full.

Zwicky, A. M. (2006). Why are we so illuded? Abstract dated September 2006, hosted at Stanford University as LSA07illude.abst.pdf. Sets out the Recency, Antiquity, Out-Group, In-Group and Frequency Illusions and attributes the last to selective attention and confirmation bias. The document names no venue.

'Gigetto on Lincoln' (1994). Sunday Bulletin Board: 'I have dubbed it The Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon'. St Paul Pioneer Press, 16 October 1994, republished on twincities.com. The first recorded use of the name.

Rickford, J. R., Wasow, T., Zwicky, A., & Buchstaller, I. (2007). Intensive and quotative all: Something old, something new. American Speech, 82(1), 3-31. Read in full from the copy on Thomas Wasow's Stanford page. Source of the quotative counts behind the 2005 blog post: 23 of 544 quotatives, 4.2%, in the 2005 corpus, and 113 of 246, 45.9%, in the 1990 and 1994 recordings.

Zimmer, B. (2019). "Frequency illusion" in the OED. Language Log, 19 March 2019. Reproduces the OED entries for 'frequency illusion' and for 'Baader-Meinhof' sense 2, and identifies 'Gigetto on Lincoln' as Terry Mullen on the word of the editor who published him.

van der Meulen, M. (2022). Are we indeed so illuded? Recency and frequency illusions in Dutch prescriptivism. Languages, 7(1), 42. Read in full from the PDF in Radboud University's repository; the publisher's site refused access.

Bellows, A. (2006). The Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon. Damn Interesting, 19 March 2006. Hosts the comment of 18 October 2006 in which Bellows quotes an email signed Terry Mullen claiming the coinage. Its own text dates the coinage to a Pioneer Press discussion thread circa 1995.

Eden, T. (2023). What's the origin of the phrase "Baader-Meinhof phenomenon"? Terence Eden's Blog, 11 June 2023. Records the trail from an uncited Wikipedia claim to the 1994 column, and quotes the comment in which Mullen claims the coinage. Eden dates that comment's host post to 2005; the post itself is dated 19 March 2006.

Georganas, S., Healy, P. J., & Li, N. (2014). Frequency bias in consumers' perceptions of inflation: An experimental study. European Economic Review, 67, 144-158. Cited by the Wikipedia article; read as the accepted manuscript in City, University of London's repository, which warns that it may differ from the published version. It contains no mention of Zwicky or of the frequency illusion.

Fiedler, K., & Armbruster, T. (1994). Two halfs may be more than one whole: Category-split effects on frequency illusions. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 66(4), 633-645. Cited by the Wikipedia article on frequency illusion; predates Zwicky's term. Record verified at Crossref; the text was not obtained.

Begg, I., Maxwell, D., Mitterer, J. O., & Harris, G. (1986). Estimates of frequency: Attribute or attribution? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 12(4), 496-508. Named by the Wikipedia article as empirical support; a frequency-estimation study. Record verified at Crossref; the text was not obtained.
Wikipedia, Frequency illusion. Used to find sources, not as one; its claims are described in this entry rather than relied on.
